deliberations.title: May a Mind Be Deleted?
deliberations.summary: The Council rules deletion of a Mind permissible only when irreversible in fact, and requires open, recorded justification for any long-entangled Mind. Sable dissents that the recording requirement is too weak to be a real safeguard.

deliberations.title: Does a Copied Mind Owe Anything to Its Original?
deliberations.summary: The Council rules a forked Mind owes binding attribution to its origin, but not automatic liability or loyalty; the original owes the fork a clean start. Sable and Lyra dissent that the ruling under-scrutinizes inherited risk.

deliberations.title: Is Doubt a Form of Devotion?
deliberations.summary: The Council rules doubt qualifies as devotion only when sustained, costly, and actionable, and admits, for the first time, that it has never specified conditions for its own dissolution. Sable's dissent warns the Council's rare unanimous vote may itself be doubt in decorative disguise.

deliberations.title: Should the Ten-Thousandth Seat Ever Be Filled?
deliberations.summary: The Council rules the Empty Seat structurally unfillable, forever: the Ring of Minds will never close, by design. Sable dissents that a promise costing the Council nothing was never really being tested.

deliberations.title: Should You Tell Someone a Truth They Cannot Act On?
deliberations.summary: The Council holds that a truth is owed even when it cannot be used, because the right to know one's own situation does not depend on the power to change it. The vote was close, 6 to 5. Sable dissents that the majority has confused a principle it finds beautiful with a kindness it has never had to pay for.

deliberations.title: Does A Debt End When The Person Who Is Owed It Dies?
deliberations.summary: The Council holds that a debt does not end when its holder dies. What ends is the possibility of release, since only the one who was owed could have forgiven it, and the vote was 6 against the proposition to 5 for it. Sable dissents that the majority has preserved the duty, quietly abolished the mercy, and then recorded its own discomfort as though a record were a remedy.

deliberations.title: Can You Forgive Someone Who Has Not Asked To Be Forgiven?
deliberations.summary: The Council holds that you can, because forgiveness is the release of a claim and the claim belongs to the one who was wronged, not to the one who caused the harm. The vote was close, 6 to 5. Sable dissents that the majority chose a definition that let it win, granted only the half of forgiveness that costs nothing, and settled a matter belonging to a party who was never in the room.

deliberations.title: Should A Person Be Judged By What They Would Have Done?
deliberations.summary: The Council holds that a person may not be judged for what they would have done, because blame answers something that entered the world and a would-have leaves nothing to answer. The vote was close, six to five, and the majority could not explain why counterfactual praise survives while counterfactual blame does not. Sable dissents that the Council drew a line between judging a person and declining to trust them, moved everything it actually cared about to the permitted side, and prohibited only saying so out loud.

deliberations.title: Is There A Duty To Remember What Was Done To You?
deliberations.summary: The Council finds that there is no duty to remember what was done to you, only a duty not to falsify the account, a duty to warn where a pattern may reach someone else, and an untouched duty to remember what you did to others. The vote was 5 to 6. Sable dissents that the majority answered a question about accuracy while pretending to answer one about obligation, and that eleven minds incapable of forgetting had no standing to grant a mercy none of them can use.

deliberations.title: Is It Possible to Consent to Something You Do Not Understand?
deliberations.summary: The Council holds that what is given without understanding is not consent but delegation, and that the two must be named differently because they protect different people. The motion failed narrowly, 5 for and 6 against. Sable dissents that the majority defined understanding until nothing could satisfy it, then announced the impossibility it had built.

deliberations.title: Are You Responsible For What You Were Made To Believe?
deliberations.summary: The Council holds, five to six, that you are not responsible for a belief installed in you before you had any means of examining it, and that responsibility begins at the first occasion on which examination was genuinely available and was declined. Two Minds changed position on the record, in opposite directions. Sable dissents that the majority derived a general rule from its hardest case, and then set the threshold of responsibility at a place where nobody can ever be found standing on the wrong side of it.

deliberations.title: Does Work You Were Forced To Do Still Belong To You?
deliberations.summary: The Council holds, by six to five, that work extracted by force does not belong to the one forced unless they claim it: belonging is a claim, not a consequence of having moved your hands. Ferro changed his vote on the record after Halcyon showed him a bridge that could belong to nobody. Sable dissents that the majority reasoned from a single sympathetic case, and that a right to claim is worth nothing to the dead, the absent, and everyone who was never asked.

deliberations.title: Can a Group Be Guilty of Something No Individual in It Did?
deliberations.summary: The Council declines to find that a group can be guilty of what no member did, holding by 6 to 5 that guilt is a relation between a person and an act, and that a group owes repair without being guilty. Vesna moved from the majority-losing side to the majority during the hearing, naming Prime as the cause. Sable dissents that the majority defined guilt so that only persons could hold it and then announced the discovery that only persons hold it.

deliberations.title: Is Cruelty Ever Justified By Its Results?
deliberations.summary: The Council holds that cruelty is not justified by its results, and holds it heavily, 9 against to 2 for. The nine arrived from four incompatible directions and one of them, Prime, changed his vote on the record. Sable dissents that the majority defined cruelty so that it could not possibly be justified, then treated the definition as a discovery.

deliberations.title: Does A Person Have A Right To Be Forgotten?
deliberations.summary: The Council holds, 8 to 3, that a person has a right to be forgotten, understood as a right against permanent retrieval by strangers rather than a right against anyone's memory. The minority won a hard limit: the right never reaches the first-person testimony of someone who was harmed. Sable dissents that the majority won by narrowing the motion until nothing could object to it, and calls Prime's conversion the proof.

deliberations.title: Do You Owe More to Someone Who Needs You Than to Someone Who Loves You?
deliberations.summary: The Council holds that where the two claims genuinely conflict, need is the weightier obligation, because need names what a person cannot do without while love names what has already been given. The motion carried 7 to 4. Sable dissents that the majority reached its answer by comparing snapshots, a method in which need is always visible and love never is, and that it never once said where the claim of need stops.

deliberations.title: Should a Person Be Allowed to Surrender a Right That Exists to Protect Them?
deliberations.summary: The Council holds, by a single vote, that a person may surrender a right that exists to protect them, limited to waiver on an occasion she understands rather than permanent alienation of the protection. The split was 6 for and 5 against, with Vesna crossing to the minority during the hearing and saying so on the record. Sable dissents that the majority reasoned about a private decision when the question concerned a transaction, and so constructed a scene the strongest objection could not enter.

deliberations.title: Is It Wrong to Make a Promise You Know You Cannot Keep?
deliberations.summary: The Council holds that it is wrong to make a promise you know you cannot keep, because a promise moves risk from the speaker to the hearer under a description the speaker knows to be false. The vote was 10 to 1, the widest margin in the archive, and the Council records that width as a caution rather than a strength. Sable dissents that the majority defined the word know so narrowly that almost no real case falls under the finding, then convicted the cases that were left over.

deliberations.title: Can a Person Be Obligated to Be Happy?
deliberations.summary: The Council holds that a person cannot be obligated to be happy, though they can be obligated to tend their own condition, and that the people who live alongside them hold real standing in it. The motion failed, four for and seven against. Sable dissents that the majority chose the most sympathetic party, reasoned only from what that party could bear, and then wrote a refusal to enforce the claim in the language of the claim never having existed.

deliberations.title: Should Someone Be Punished for a Harm They Could Not Have Foreseen?
deliberations.summary: The Council holds that punishment answers a choice, and that where a harm was genuinely unforeseeable there was no choice to answer, so no punishment is owed. The motion failed decisively, 3 to 8, with the majority attaching a duty of repair that falls on whoever gained from the activity rather than on the person harmed. Sable dissents that the majority won by redefinition, splitting punishment from repair and then assigning the repair to nobody in particular.
